semantic_reviews.reconstruction_test: question_6_learner_test: ["OBJ-6116-3.3.1-08 / ITEM-6116-3-149-SYNTH (5 marks): from 'Investigating diffusion along a tube' alone the answer is: IV distance from the source; DV time to turn blue; controls of the same litmus, wetness, tube and temperature; the clock starts when the teacher places the ammonia pad; repeat and take a mean at each distance. This earns 5/5.", "OBJ-6116-3.6.2.3-03 / ITEM-6116-3-325-MECH (4 marks): from 'The digestion of starch' alone the answer is: salivary amylase turns starch to maltose in the mouth; stomach acid inhibits it; pancreatic amylase continues in the small intestine; maltase on the lining gives glucose for absorption. This earns 4/4.", "Flashcards ITEM-6116-3-127-DIST, -141-PROC, -168-DEF, -190-PROC, -230-FEATURE and -312-DEF can all be answered from the notes alone. ITEM-6116-3-P03 (10 marks) is also fully supported by the worked example and 'Making the results trustworthy'."] question_7_misconceptions: All 8 MISCON items (464, 465, 466, 469, 472, 475, 476, 477) are error-correction items quoting the wrong idea, so the learner must reject it and give the right one. All discriminate. 469 names 'mineral-condition pairings', a mild cue. 472 cues the answer with 'using the active site' (3AB-009). None restates a bare definition.

issues.finding: The second marking point and the canonical answer justify "light was not limiting at the plateau" with an invalid reason. Light intensity being the same for both curves does not show that light was not limiting. What shows it is that the first curve is flat there, so more light gave no rise in rate. What shows carbon dioxide was limiting is that raising carbon dioxide alone raised the rate. The mark scheme credits a non-sequitur as the reason.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners learn that a factor held equal between two treatments is "not limiting". That is the reasoning the notes warn against in "Identify the active limit", where a flat curve alone does not identify the limit.
issues.recommended_repair: Rewrite mark 2 as: "the first curve is flat (level) at high light, so extra light did not raise the rate and light was not limiting; raising carbon dioxide alone did raise it, so carbon dioxide was the limiting factor." Make the canonical answer match.
issues.resolution: ITEM-6116-3-258-APP: mark 2 and canonical answer now argue that the first curve is flat at high light (extra light gave no rise, so light not limiting) and that raising carbon dioxide alone raised the rate (so carbon dioxide limiting). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The boiled-saliva control in the notes is interpreted with the exact word the examiners penalise ("destroyed", MISCON-6116-021: "killed" or "destroyed" instead of "denatured"). The inference is also back to front. The control does not show that boiling destroyed the enzyme, which is assumed. It shows that the starch loss in the first tube needed active enzyme, not some other part of saliva or the conditions.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners copy "destroyed by boiling" into exam answers and lose the denaturation mark. They also learn to describe what a control assumes instead of what it shows.
issues.recommended_repair: Replace with: "Boiling denatures amylase, so the boiled-saliva tube shows that the starch disappeared in the first tube because of active enzyme, not because of anything else in saliva or the conditions."
issues.resolution: 3.6.2.3-03 'The digestion of starch': boiled-saliva control now says boiling denatures amylase and the control shows starch loss needed active enzyme, not anything else in saliva or the conditions. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: OBJ-6116-3.5-06 requires investigating the effect of temperature and pH on lipase as well as amylase. The notes give a full amylase method but only one sentence on lipase, that fatty acids lower pH and can be followed with an indicator. The notes then say an indicator endpoint cannot be compared across pH values, and offer no workable alternative. A learner has no lipase method for either factor, for example milk or cream with lipase and sodium carbonate and phenolphthalein, timed until the pink disappears, at different temperatures.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner asked to plan a lipase temperature investigation cannot write the substrate, indicator, endpoint or controls from the notes. The pH caveat may leave them thinking lipase cannot be investigated at all.
issues.recommended_repair: Add a short lipase method with a temperature series (milk, sodium carbonate, phenolphthalein, time to colour loss, boiled-lipase control, equal volumes, water baths). Restate the pH caveat with what to do instead, for example measuring pH change with a meter or probe rather than a fixed indicator colour.
issues.resolution: 3.5-06 notes: replaced the bare pH caveat with a lipase temperature method (milk or cream, sodium carbonate, phenolphthalein, pre-equilibrated water baths, time to loss of pink, equal volumes, boiled-lipase control) and said what to do for pH instead (measure pH change over a fixed time with a meter or probe). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: Water absorption is taught unconditionally as osmosis "from the more dilute gut contents into the more concentrated blood". The cholera section in the same unit correctly teaches the reverse, where raised gut solute concentration draws water into the gut. The condition, that water is absorbed because solutes are absorbed and so the gut contents are the more dilute side, is dropped in the water-absorption section.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner may treat gut contents as always more dilute than blood. They then cannot explain why the direction reverses in cholera, or after a very salty or sugary load.
issues.recommended_repair: Condition the sentence: "Normally, as digested food and ions are absorbed, the gut contents become more dilute than the blood, so water follows by osmosis; if solutes build up in the gut, as in cholera, water moves the other way."
issues.resolution: 3.6.2.4-08 'Water absorption' claim conditioned: gut contents become more dilute as food and ions are absorbed, so water follows by osmosis; reverses if solutes build up, as in cholera. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: Part (b) asks for the solution in which cells "neither gain nor lose water". The notes stress that water crosses in both directions and that there is "no net movement" in an isotonic solution. The stem drops "net".
issues.educational_consequence: The wording supports the misconception that water stops moving at equilibrium. The answer, isotonic, is unaffected.
issues.recommended_repair: Reword to "...in which the onion cells show no net gain or loss of water".
issues.resolution: Post-review repair: exemplar generator now asks for cells that show no net gain or loss of water. Exemplar and topic 3 were regenerated; structural checks pass. This is an author resolution, not a second reviewer verdict.

issues.finding: "Warmth and water switch the enzymes on" is loose. Water uptake triggers enzyme activity and production. Warmth only affects the rate, and germination also needs oxygen. The sentence presents temperature as an on/off switch, which contradicts the unit's own teaching that low temperature only slows enzymes.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners may write that a cold seed's enzymes are "off", or leave oxygen out of the germination conditions taught in 4.3.5.
issues.recommended_repair: Say: "Water taken up by the seed activates its enzymes; a suitable temperature lets them work at a useful rate. A dry seed's enzymes are inactive, which is why it can be stored for years."
issues.resolution: 3.5-07 notes: 'Warmth and water switch the enzymes on' replaced with: water uptake activates the enzymes, a suitable temperature lets them work at a useful rate, enzymes in a dry seed are inactive. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The objective names "epithelium of mammalian trachea" as an example slide. The notes describe epithelium only as "cells packed together as a covering layer" and never mention the ciliated cells or goblet cells a learner would see and label on a trachea slide.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner drawing a trachea slide has no guidance on what to look for or label.
issues.recommended_repair: Add one sentence that tracheal epithelium shows column-shaped cells with cilia on the free surface and scattered mucus-secreting (goblet) cells, cross-referenced to 3.9.
issues.resolution: 3.2-04 notes: added that tracheal epithelium has column-shaped ciliated cells with scattered mucus-secreting goblet cells, cross-referenced to 3.9. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The stem asks "which mineral treatment is supported". The marking credits identifying the cause of paleness (iron shortage) and iron's role in chlorophyll, not a treatment, so the question and the marked answer do not match.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner may answer "add iron" and stop, missing both marks, which need the evidence and the chlorophyll link.
issues.recommended_repair: Reword to "Explain what these results show about the cause of the pale leaves."
issues.resolution: ITEM-6116-3-233-APP stem reworded to 'Explain what these seedling results show about the cause of the pale leaves.' Command word unchanged; guidance already matched. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The stem "Explain the error using the active site" points learners to the shape change, so it partly gives the answer away. A learner who holds the "killed" misconception is still steered to the active-site account. The item does test the denature-versus-kill distinction, but weakly.
issues.educational_consequence: Weaker discrimination of MISCON-6116-021 than the other misconception items.
issues.recommended_repair: Drop "using the active site", or ask for the word that should replace "kills" and what it means.
issues.resolution: ITEM-6116-3-472-MISCON (3.5-04) stem no longer cues 'using the active site': now asks what is wrong with 'kills the enzyme' and what boiling actually does. Answer and 2-mark guidance unchanged. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

semantic_reviews.reconstruction_test: q6_learner_test: OBJ-6116-3.10.1-06 (ITEM-012, 5 marks): written from notes 3.10.1 alone: separate samples in water baths at 15, 25 and 35 °C; equilibrate; droplet distance per minute with CO2 absorbent; same species, mass, hydration and germination stage; repeat with fresh samples and compare. This earns 5/5. "Mean" is implied rather than explicit in 3.10.1. OBJ-6116-3.14-04 (ITEM-116, 4 marks): hypothalamus detects the fall in blood temperature; arterioles narrow; shivering releases heat; raised hairs trap air. This earns 4/4. Sampled short-answer items (ITEM-008, 076, 406, 415, 416, 424) can all be answered from the notes alone. ITEM-387 is the exception: its narrow-lumen point is not in the notes (3CD-007). q7_misconceptions: Every misconception item uses an "explain the error" stem, so the stem always says the statement is wrong. Discriminating: 463 (iris vs ciliary), 468 (condom), 474 (nucleated cell), 478 (urea vs bile), 479 (retina) and 470 (mesophyll site; the "how it leaves" half is cued). 462 discriminates moderately: the bile attributes are in the stem, but the learner must supply pancreas, blood and glucose. Weak: 467 and 480, which are binary inversions (3CD-005). Stem gives the answer away: 471, 473, and half of 481 (3CD-004).

issues.finding: Objective OBJ-6116-3.13.1-05 asks learners to "describe the effects of alcohol on the release of the neurotransmitter". The notes never connect alcohol to transmitter release. They say only that alcohol "slows synaptic transmission". The one sentence about blocked release, in the synapse section, is about an unnamed chemical and is not linked to alcohol. The expected point is that alcohol reduces or slows neurotransmitter release at synapses, so impulses in the next neurone are delayed or fewer.
issues.educational_consequence: Asked about alcohol and neurotransmitter release, a learner can only say "slows transmission" and cannot name the step affected. That answer is likely to lose the mark that depends on release.
issues.recommended_repair: In 3.13.1 Alcohol and synaptic signalling, add one sentence: alcohol reduces (slows) the release of neurotransmitter at synapses, so less transmitter crosses the gap and the next neurone is stimulated more slowly. Keep the ITEM-481 wording consistent with it.
issues.resolution: 3.13.1 Alcohol and synaptic signalling: claim and body now state alcohol reduces neurotransmitter release, so less transmitter crosses the gap and the next neurone is stimulated more slowly. 3.13.1-05 FEATURE answer/guidance and ITEM-481 made consistent. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: Both sub-topic cross-references in the 3.7 connector point to the wrong place. In the objective registry, 3.6.1.1 is leaf structure and 3.6.1.2 is mineral ions; the photosynthesis equation and rate objectives are 3.6.1.3. The note says the reverse, and it also cites a numbering that the notes file does not use: its headings stop at "3.6.1 Photosynthesis and plant nutrition".
issues.educational_consequence: A learner who follows the reference to revise leaf anatomy lands on mineral-deficiency content. A learner looking for photosynthesis lands on leaf structure.
issues.recommended_repair: Change to "Leaf anatomy is in 3.6.1.1" and "covered in 3.6.1.3", or cite the heading names in 3.6.1.
issues.resolution: 3.7 connector now cites the heading '3.6.1 Photosynthesis and plant nutrition' for both leaf anatomy and photosynthesis; wrong 3.6.1.1/3.6.1.2 references removed. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The worked example credits adrenaline with supplying the energy for a movement that is over before adrenaline can act. Stepping back from a car takes a fraction of a second and is a nervous response. Adrenaline is secreted into the blood and acts afterwards, raising pulse rate and blood glucose to support continued activity. The example also contradicts the notes' own rule in 3.13.1: nervous responses are rapid, hormonal responses are slower.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners may explain an instant avoiding movement by adrenaline, mixing up nervous and hormonal coordination. This is exactly the comparison that OBJ-6116-3.13.1-22 tests.
issues.recommended_repair: Reframe the example: the quick step is a nervous response. Adrenaline released at the same time keeps pulse rate and blood glucose raised for the following seconds to minutes, for example while the person runs on or stays alert. Say that the hormonal effect follows the nervous one.
issues.resolution: 3.13.3 worked example reframed: the step back is a nervous response; adrenaline is secreted at the same time and its effects (pulse, blood glucose) follow over seconds to minutes while the runner keeps running or stays alert. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: These misconception items give away the answer in the stem. 471 and 473 each name exactly two agents and two effects, say the pairing is wrong, and ask for it to be reassigned. A learner can earn both marks by swapping the pairs, with no biology needed. In 481 the stem itself says lung damage "happens with smoking", which is the whole content of mark 1. None of the three makes the learner choose between the right idea and the wrong one.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners who still hold the misconception score full or half marks. The items then report the misconception as cleared when it is not.
issues.recommended_repair: Use the discriminating tests in misconceptions.json. For 020, ask which smoke component reduces oxygen carried by blood and which damages cilia, without pairing them in the stem. For 022, give one cargo and ask for the tissue and direction. For 041, remove "as happens with smoking" and ask which organ system alcohol acts on to slow reactions.
issues.resolution: ITEM-471 (3.9-11) and ITEM-473 (3.7-04) fixed. Stems no longer state the swapped pairing. 3.9-11: learner claims tar does both jobs and must say which part is wrong (CO binds haemoglobin) and name tar for the cilia. 3.7-04: learner claims one tissue carries both water and sucrose and must name xylem and phloem. Guidance is one point per mark. ITEM-481 is not mine (3D). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: These are binary inversions with the error flagged in the stem. Reversing the stated equation, or negating each stated condition (tight to slack, thin to thick), gives most of the answer. Each needs one small piece of knowledge: that the reversed equation is photosynthesis, and that the stated conditions are those for distant vision. They discriminate only weakly.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner who mixes up near and distant accommodation can still score by negating each condition.
issues.recommended_repair: For 039, ask what the ciliary muscles do for a near object and what follows, so the learner must produce the sequence. For 012, ask for the reactants of respiration with no equation given.
issues.resolution: ITEM-467: no equation in stem; student uses the photosynthesis reactants and the learner must name them and give the respiration equation. ITEM-480: stem now says ciliary muscles relax for near vision; learner must correct it and produce the ligament and lens sequence. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The marking guidance makes an absolute claim that the notes do not teach and that is not strictly true: blood glucose rises "only" when liver glycogen is broken down. Adrenaline also mobilises other reserves. The item works at this level because the stem tells the learner that blood glucose does not rise, but the "only" is unnecessary.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners take away a false absolute: that glycogen breakdown is the sole route by which blood glucose can rise.
issues.recommended_repair: Change to "adrenaline raises blood glucose mainly by causing the liver to break down glycogen; with no glycogen store, it cannot do this".
issues.resolution: ITEM-110 guidance: 'only' removed; now 'adrenaline raises blood glucose mainly by causing the liver to break down glycogen'. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The marking guidance credits "a narrow lumen helps keep the pressure high" as a linked adaptation. The notes never make that link: they say only that a narrow lumen "accompanies" the strong wall. A learner cannot learn this creditable point from the notes. The point is also weak physiologically.
issues.educational_consequence: The notes and the mark scheme do not agree on which artery features earn credit.
issues.recommended_repair: Either drop the lumen point from the guidance or state it, with its function, in the notes.
issues.resolution: Narrow-lumen point removed from the ITEM-387 (3.8.1-03) guidance. The three remaining linked features (thick wall, elastic tissue, smooth muscle) are all taught in the 3.8.1 Arteries notes. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The effect of selective weedkillers is first stated without its condition ("leave grasses and cereals unharmed"). The dose and species condition comes only in the following sentence. The key-point line has the condition ("at the intended dose"); the body sentence does not.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner may memorise the absolute claim that weedkillers never harm grasses.
issues.recommended_repair: Change to "at the recommended dose they kill broad-leaved weeds ... while grasses and cereals are largely unaffected".
issues.resolution: 3.12 body now reads 'at the recommended dose they kill broad-leaved weeds ... while grasses and cereals are largely unaffected'; 3.12-05 WHY answer and guidance aligned. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The objective asks for the effects of nicotine "on the gas exchange system". The notes give only dependence and cardiovascular effects, and they say outright that these are different from airway damage. This is defensible, but the notes do not explain how these effects fit an objective about the gas exchange system. A learner may think the answer is off-topic.
issues.educational_consequence: The learner is unsure what to write for a nicotine question set under gas exchange.
issues.recommended_repair: Add one line: nicotine's main contribution is addiction, which keeps the smoker exposed to tar and carbon monoxide that damage the gas exchange system. Its direct effects are mainly on the heart and blood vessels.
issues.resolution: 3.9 Nicotine notes: replaced the 'different from tar/CO' sentence with one that links nicotine to the gas exchange system through addiction, which keeps the smoker breathing in tar and carbon monoxide. Word count stays within budget. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

blockers: No deterministic opinion on 3 checks (C-35, C-41, C-43) - on these a human or model reviewer is the only line of defence.

notes: Standard v0.2.0-draft check suite. 44 checks: 39 pass, 0 fail, 2 warn, 3 not_run.
A not_run check means an input the check needs is absent. It is never a pass.
RS-30: these are mechanical results computed by code. They say nothing about whether the material teaches the subject well.
